sections.content: You know *desde hace* from A2 Unit 7: *Estudio español desde hace tres años*. Spanish has a second way to say it, with *llevar*: *Llevo tres años estudiando español*. You know *estar* + gerund from A1 Unit 19 (*estoy estudiando*). In this pattern *llevar* takes the place of *estar*, and the length of time comes straight after it, with no word for "for" in between. The action began in the past and is still going on now. Because the time comes first, this is the natural choice when you want to stress how long something has taken, or how much effort it has cost.
sections.title: How long has it been going on?
llevar + length of time + gerund
rows: I have been studying Spanish for three years.
Llevamos una hora esperando el autobús.
We have been waiting for the bus for an hour.
How long have you been working here?
Mi hermana lleva mucho tiempo buscando casa.
My sister has been looking for a house for a long time.

sections.title: In the past, and with sin

items.spanish: Llevábamos una hora esperando cuando llegó el tren.
items.english: We had been waiting for an hour when the train arrived.

items.spanish: Llevo una semana sin dormir bien.
items.english: I have not slept well for a week.

sections.content: The verb after the time is always a gerund: *estudiando*, never *estudiar* or *estudiado*. To say how long you have gone without doing something, use *sin* + infinitive: *Llevo una semana sin dormir bien*, not *Llevo una semana no durmiendo*. Use *llevar* only for something that is still going on; for a finished action, use the preterite: *Estudié tres años*.
